title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
summary: Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress urges staff forward and offers pay raises after Jensen Huang exit.
body: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high. Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday. Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject. The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up." Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands. Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

title: Fed officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI impact on inflation, minutes show
summary: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday released minutes from its October policy meeting at which it voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%.
body: Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk." More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December. The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective." In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December. Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability. Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint." "Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms." Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off. Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal." Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target. The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach. However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act. At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

title: Is Apple the safe haven investors think it is? Here's a way to trade it with less risk
summary: Traders have flocked to Apple's perceived safety in the wake of Nvidia's scandal. It may not be so safe, says Mike Khouw
body: For months, Apple has been the undisputed haven of the technology sector. As the industry grappled with the brutal reality of Nvidia's post-Huang future, investors blindly rotated into Apple, comforting themselves with the narrative that the Cupertino giant was uniquely immune to speculative overspending on artificial intelligence. While peers bled capital into server farms and data centers. At almost 37x forward earnings estimates, the stock is now priced for perfection, fully valued at precisely the moment the rest of the market is beginning to see multiples contract aggressively. Investors tend to huddle in the shelter of perceived safe havens, but that perceived safety can crack quickly in an adverse news cycle, as Nvidia shareholders recently learned. We've recently witnessed a bizarre parade of catastrophic system failures: the massive Microsoft outage, the FAA grounding flights, and cascading disruptions across major banking networks. Through it all, Apple was immune. Until today, when a widespread outage struck, knocking out iCloud, Apple Pay, and core support systems. The official explanation? Yet another internal update gone wrong. It's undeniably odd how all these major tech infrastructure failures are being chalked up to routine upgrades, all clustering around the exact same narrow timeframe. Without venturing too far into the conspiratorial, the sheer coincidence of these cascading digital blackouts suggests more systemic fragility than we may have realized. That's one thing at less than 10x forward earnings, as Nvidia is, or even at a market multiple. But Apple is twice as expensive as the S&P. Technically, Apple is balancing on a knife's edge. Shares have been relentlessly hugging the upper end of several channel-based technical indicators, such as the Bollinger Band. Apple has been priced at a steep premium for being immune to what ails other struggling stocks, but is now demonstrating similar vulnerabilities. Investors should ask themselves: what's the upside? That Apple trades at more than 40x forward earnings? 45x? Even at that rich multiple, that would represent only 18-19% upside from here. If the market suddenly decided that Apple's premium to the market would be just 50%, instead of 100%, that would be less than 28x forward earnings, a nearly 27% haircut to the current share price. Despite the high multiple, options prices are low versus the market. Market implied volatility is well above average (around the 93rd percentile). Apple implied volatility is actually just below the 1-year average. The price of index options is in the 98th percentile relative to Apple options. Because the stock is nominally expensive (translation? The share price is high in dollar terms), buying outright naked puts is highly capital-intensive. This is exactly where a put spread makes sense. By buying an at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money put and simultaneously selling a lower-strike put, traders can dramatically reduce the upfront capital cost. More importantly, this structure blunts the negative impact of theta, or time decay, ensuring you don't bleed premium while waiting for the technical breakdown to materialize. Furthermore, taking advantage of the natural put skew—where further out-of-the-money puts trade at relatively higher implied volatility—lets you finance your bearish bet efficiently by selling that inflated premium. Apple's historic premium is built on a foundation of immunity to the chaos infecting the rest of the market. Today's outage proved the company may be more vulnerable than investors appreciate. body: A stable Aa1 outlook removes one source of headline risk for Treasuries, but the growth upgrade cuts the other way for bonds. Stronger-than-expected activity strengthens the hawkish case being made by Fed officials this week and supports pricing for a December hike, which should keep front-end yields and the dollar firm. That’s a headwind for gold, which has tended to fall as Fed hike expectations build. Moody’s flagged energy prices as a drag on growth, a reminder that oil is the swing factor: further strength in crude would hurt growth and keep inflation pressure alive at the same time. Moody’s says the US economy has outperformed, and it’s leaving the rating alone. But it expects the things that drove this year’s strength, cheap money aside, to fade as higher rates, costly energy and a maturing AI boom slow growth to about 2%. Moody’s Ratings said the US economy has performed better than it initially expected in 2026, and it kept the country’s Aa1 sovereign rating with a stable outlook in its regular review of US creditworthiness. The agency pointed to real GDP growth of 3.4% at an annualised pace in the third quarter and now expects growth of 2.3% for the full year, before a slowdown to around 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Artificial intelligence features on both sides of that outlook. Moody’s said heavy spending on AI infrastructure is propping up growth in the near term and could eventually deliver lasting productivity gains, although it stressed that the size of those gains is still uncertain. At the same time, it expects the AI investment cycle to normalise, which would remove some of the support that has driven this year’s outperformance. The agency listed two other headwinds alongside that: higher interest rates and energy prices that remain elevated. Both are live issues. Several Federal Reserve officials have argued this week for further tightening, and oil markets remain on edge over shipping risks in the Middle East. Against those pressures, Moody’s said the economy’s capacity for innovation, a dynamic private sector and deep capital markets should continue to support investment and productivity over time. The rating rationale leans heavily on institutional strengths. Moody’s cited the country’s very high creditworthiness, its resilience to shocks and the dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency. It also said it expects the US to maintain its long record of effective monetary policy led by an independent Federal Reserve. That point is more than a formality: Fed independence is one of the pillars the rating rests on, so any perceived erosion of it would sit squarely within what the agency is watching. For investors, the review offers reassurance without much drama. A stable outlook signals that Moody’s sees no near-term pressure for a change in either direction, and its growth forecasts broadly match the picture of an economy that is running hotter than expected but set to cool as rates bite and the AI spending surge matures. A solid headline gain plus a steady or lower jobless rate would likely bring back some pricing for a February hike and lift the Aussie off its lows. A rise in unemployment to 4.8% or higher would probably extend the slide and pull front-end yields lower as traders price a longer peak. The minutes flagged that oil costs tied to the Middle East conflict could add to inflation, which means a soft print alone may not close the door on further tightening while crude stays elevated. --- Australia’s jobs report should recover most of September’s part-time losses, but with a divided RBA board split over how close the economy is to a sharper downturn, the unemployment rate matters more than the headline gain. Australia’s October labour force report lands at 00:30 GMT on Thursday (7:30 pm US Eastern on Wednesday), and it arrives with more riding on it than a typical monthly print. Economists expect employment to have risen by around 25,000 after September’s surprise 39,300 fall, with the unemployment rate seen steady at 4.7%, a five-year high, and participation unchanged at 66.8%. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics last month showed the decline was driven almost entirely by a 73,700 slump in part-time roles, while full-time jobs actually rose by about 34,000. That split is the heart of the case for a rebound. CBA expects the part-time drop to reverse, arguing that large swings in part-time work have historically unwound the following month. Its own internal labour data point to October growth of around 18,000, which it describes as a touch below the pace needed to keep unemployment from rising. In other words, even a healthy-looking headline gain could leave the jobless rate drifting higher. The release follows two days of mixed signals for the Reserve Bank of Australia. Minutes published on Tuesday showed six of nine board members backed November’s 25 basis point hike to 4.85%, the fifth increase of 2026 and the highest cash rate since 2008, judging policy not yet clearly tight enough to contain upside inflation risks. The three dissenters warned the economy might be close to a materially sharper downturn, pointing to the delayed effect of earlier hikes, a bigger-than-expected rise in unemployment and a softening housing market. Wednesday then brought September quarter wages up 1.1%, the largest quarterly gain since late 2023, lifting annual growth to 3.5%, although real wages have now gone backwards for four straight quarters with inflation above 4%. The data matter because they speak directly to that split. A jobless rate stuck at 4.7%, or lower, would support the majority view that the labour market is loosening only gradually, which Westpac also expects as jobs growth runs below population growth. A rise to 4.8% or beyond would hand the dissenters fresh evidence and make it harder for the hawks to argue for a sixth hike. Several high-profile layoff announcements, including job cuts at NAB, Qantas, Rio Tinto and David Jones, add to the sense of downside risk, though economists note the numbers remain small relative to average monthly hiring. The RBA’s own forecasts already assume unemployment climbs, reaching 4.9% by the end of this year and a bit above 5% by late 2028, so a modest uptick would not be a shock. For some, however, the very fact of production growth in the Permian is a surprise. The Permian has been the engine driving U.S. crude oil output growth for over a decade. Annual growth in the past consistently exceeded 1 million barrels--until 2020, when pandemic lockdowns killed demand and plunged U.S. crude into negative territory briefly. Since then, shale production growth and Permian production growth specifically have moderated. The basin spanning Texas and New Mexico still accounts for about 45% of the U.S. national total in crude and is the biggest contributor to total production growth. Yet even the war premium on prices this year has not been enough to convince shale drillers to drill, baby, drill. Enverus expects the country’s total crude oil production to rise by 378,000 barrels daily, with most of that coming from the Permian. The number is not particularly impressive compared to previous annual output jumps that were in the six figures but, Bloomberg noted in a report on the forecast, this would represent an annual increase of 2.8%, versus a much smaller annual production increase of 1.6% for 2025 versus 2024. The war premium, in other words, may have motivated Permian operators to ramp up drilling. “There’s a ton of operators that are just adding a little bit — which then on aggregate makes a big change,” Enverus analyst Stephen Sagriff told the publication. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates According to the Energy Information Administration , crude oil production in the Permian averaged 6.84 million barrels daily in the third quarter of the year, a modest increase on the second quarter when the Permian produced 6.82 million barrels daily. For the current quarter, the EIA expects Permian operators to ramp up further to 6.91 million barrels daily. The forecast for 2027 is also for slow, moderate growth that would bring the Permian’s total to over 7 million barrels daily. That would be up from just 2.2 million barrels daily back in 2017. Some have warned for years that oil production in the Permian cannot continue to rise as fast as it did five years ago, not least because such fast growth comes with a price tag, and that price tag consists of higher costs as horizontal wells become longer and longer, and greater demand for fracking fluid--which then goes back into the ground and eventually creates a problem. Reports that the Permian has a wastewater problem with storage capacity running out emerged last year, indicating that production growth may remain moderate and possibly even slow down further as regulators limit new wastewater disposal licenses in response to the problem. The above confirms that no basin, conventional or otherwise, can sustain the Permian’s early years rate of production growth. This is true especially about shale oil basins where wells get drilled and put into production faster but also deplete faster--and produce inordinate amounts of wastewater, apparently. Yet others have argued that there is still plenty of oil in the Permian to continue supporting overall U.S. oil growth for years to come, possibly decades. For now, it seems the latter camp is right, despite the slower growth rate, which is quite a natural response to price movements in the past few years. The shale oil industry is doing what the rest of the oil industry is doing: making financial discipline its top priority rather than seeing just how much oil they can pump if they really put their minds--and money--to it, as shale drillers did back in the original boom days. Once superhot temperatures are reached, cold water is injected to create steam, which powers turbines. Quaise Energy says superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems. title: AngloGold outlines $2.5B Quebradona copper plan
summary: The underground project, about 60 km southwest of Medellín, could produce about 80,000 tonnes of copper a year.
body: AngloGold Ashanti (NYSE: AU; JSE: ANG) plans to spend $2.5 billion to build its Quebradona copper project in Colombia if it secures an environmental licence that has eluded the company since its first application in 2019. The underground project, about 60 km southwest of Antioquia’s capital, Medellín, could produce about 80,000 tonnes of copper a year and generate about $1.5 billion in annual exports, AngloGold said Tuesday at an investment event in New York. “We are confident that, once the environmental approvals are obtained, the project will move towards the start of construction in 2028,” Colombian Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo said in a statement issued in Spanish by AngloGold’s local unit. That timetable hinges in part on a 2025 order that created a temporary protected area covering the project and bars new environmental licences for mining in the zone while it’s in force. The restriction is due to run into mid-2028. AngloGold challenged the order in court and wrote down $98 million in project costs that year. AngloGold shares fell 7.9% to $78.01 Wednesday afternoon in New York amid global declines in mining and metals stocks. That valued the company at about $39.5 billion. AngloGold CEO Alberto Calderón told Colombia’s Blu Radio on Wednesday that he expects the licensing process to take 12 to 18 months. AngloGold could spend about $2 billion in the first two years of construction if it secures the licence, he said. Colombia’s environmental licensing agency shelved the application in 2021 after identifying gaps in the company’s studies, including on groundwater, tailings storage and potential ground subsidence. The National Mining Agency in August extended exploration to December 2027, giving AngloGold time to complete more geological, environmental and water studies. The company has begun consulting communities for a new environmental impact study. Quebradona hosts 120 million probable tonnes grading 1.23% copper for 1.47 million tonnes of contained metal, according to AngloGold’s year-end 2025 estimate. The planned plant would produce a copper concentrate with gold and silver as byproducts. title: Collective hits gold in rock classed as waste at Apollo
summary: Collective discovered gold and silver in waste rock at its Apollo deposit in Colombia, planning to invest $100M next year.
body: Collective Mining (TSX, Nasdaq: CNL) has found gold and silver in rock counted as waste inside the proposed pit at its Apollo deposit in Colombia, a day after outlining plans to spend $100 million (C$143 million) in the country next year. Of 17 holes in the shallow halo around Apollo, 15 cut intervals above the open-pit cut-off grade. All 10 holes from one drill pad hit gold and silver near surface. One cut 107.85 metres at 0.79 g/t gold and 14 g/t silver from 3.75 metres depth. A hole drilled from another pad cut 146.1 metres at 0.66 g/t gold, 19 g/t silver and 0.04% copper from 106.5 metres depth, extending below the pit floor and up to 60 metres beyond the resource boundary, Collective said Wednesday . “Overall, results suggest the pit shell understates the [shallow halo zone],” National Bank of Canada Capital Markets mining analyst Don DeMarco wrote Wednesday. Turning some of the rock already slated for removal into mill feed “could ultimately improve open-pit economics,” he said. Drilling has tested about 45% of the halo, up from 41% at the previous update, DeMarco estimated. The latest results are lower grade but cover longer intervals. Across 28 intervals in 15 holes, he calculated an average of 0.83 g/t gold-equivalent over 42.4 metres, compared with 1.18 g/t over 19.3 metres in the previous batch. Apollo is part of the Guayabales project about 80 km south of Medellín. Collective plans to test extensions beyond the pit next year, update the resource in late 2027 or early 2028 and complete its first preliminary economic assessment shortly afterwards. Next year’s spending would fund exploration and move Guayabales through licensing, executive chairman Ari Sussman said at a Colombian government event in New York on Tuesday. Collective aims to submit Apollo’s environmental licence application in the second half of 2027. Up to a further $1 billion in investment through 2030 depends on obtaining the licence, Colombian Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo said. title: Phoenix hits broad gold and copper at old BC mine
summary: The company hit broad intervals of copper and gold at Lexington in southern British Columbia.
body: Phoenix Metals (TSX: PCA) hit broad intervals of copper and gold at Lexington in southern British Columbia, where it is testing whether an old underground mining district could support an open pit. Hole LXDDH-26-001 cut 169 metres grading 1.02 grams gold, 0.22% copper and 3.79 grams silver from 41 metres depth, Phoenix said Wednesday in a statement. A second hole cut 233.5 metres at 0.26 grams gold, 0.14% copper and 0.86 grams silver from 8.5 metres depth. The company has yet to establish true widths. “These holes demonstrate the potential for Lexington to be developed into a bulk tonnage open pit target,” CEO Nick Campbell said in the release. Hole LXDDH-26-001 “demonstrates how the high-grade structures within the broad mineralized zone at Lexington can potentially upgrade gold values within a bulk tonnage target,” Miners at Lexington and the nearby City of Paris workings followed narrow, high-grade structures underground. Phoenix drilled through the surrounding rock to see how much lower-grade material might be mined alongside those structures. Its strongest hole included a higher-grade 38-metre interval. The first batch also shows how much the gold content varies across the target, with two other holes averaging 0.18 and 0.20 g/t gold over more than 180 metres each. Phoenix has traced a target over 1.5 km along strike and about 300 metres across using its drilling, surface mapping and more than 170 historical holes. That footprint is an exploration target. Testing whether it can support an open pit will require a resource estimate and an economic study. Phoenix completed 20 Lexington holes totalling 6,350 metres through October. The company expects more Lexington assays and the first results from nearby Phoenix South in December. body: US crude fell to its lowest close since August 26 on November 18, 2026, after a larger-than-expected rise in US crude and fuel stocks strengthened expectations that global oil supply would exceed demand. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures fell US$2.75, or 3.2%, to US$83.26 a barrel. Brent crude fell US$1.19, or 1.28%, to US$91.95. Both benchmarks recovered some ground before the close. WTI had been down more than US$4 a barrel during the session, while Brent had fallen by more than US$2. The war in Iran and the threat to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz helped limit the declines. US commercial crude stocks reached 417.8 million barrels in the week ending November 13, according to the US Energy Information Administration. The weekly rise of 3.4 million barrels far exceeded the 58,000 barrels forecast by analysts in a Reuters poll. US petrol stocks rose by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million, more than three times the expected increase of 1.6 million barrels. Distillate stocks, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels to 104.9 million, against a forecast rise of 1.3 million. Analysts at Gelber & Associates said the inventory figures prompted fresh selling. Attacks on commercial shipping still threatened oil deliveries through Hormuz, they said, but those risks had “provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus”. The price gap between Brent and WTI reached its widest in about two weeks on November 17, according to London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) data. US crude then fell more sharply than Brent on November 18. Both benchmarks were on course to lose about 20% in November as Middle Eastern exports rose and shipping rates fell sharply. June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, said it had become uneconomic to ship WTI to Asia and north-west Europe. body: Nvidia raised its sales forecast for its next fiscal year, and reported stronger-than-expected results in its most recent quarter, in a striking signal of business confidence by the AI chipmaker following the resignation of longtime CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang . “Our momentum is real,” interim CEO Colette Kress said on conference call with analysts on Tuesday, citing strong demand for the company’s products, Nvidia’s ongoing technological advances, and the commitment of its employees. Kress, Nvidia’s longtime finance chief, made her debut as interim CEO on Tuesday’s earnings call, flanked by newly appointed chair of the board Harvey Jones . The pair took pains to project a business-as-usual attitude—even using the phrase—while seeking to put Huang in the rear-view mirror . The board of directors “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said at the start of the call, noting that the company has retained executive recruiting firm Hedrick & Struggles to search for a permanent CEO. The comments were a direct rebuttal to Huang, who is seeking to reclaim the CEO throne just days after resigning amid revelations of multiple affairs, one reportedly with a Nvidia employee who reported to him and another with a woman some believe may be a Chinese spy. Shares of Nvidia were up more than 5% in after hours trading on Tuesday. The company’s stock has plummeted more than 36% in the past month, shedding more than a trillion dollars in market value. Investors have been spooked by the loss of Nvidia’s longtime leader, Huang, as well as by general concerns about the durability of the AI boom. Kress doused both concerns at once on Tuesday by raising sales expectations for Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 year, which is roughly equivalent to the 2027 calendar year. “We had originally indicated that we would be at about 70% growth year-over-year, and now we are are increasing that to 75%” growth,” Kress said, citing improvements in supply and ongoing strength in demand. The guidance was particularly striking because Huang himself had delivered the 70% growth forecast three months ago, framing it as an usually far-reaching forecast that reflected the exceptional strength in the business. In raising the annual revenue forecast by the equivalent of $20 billion or more, Nvidia’s message seemed to be that Huang was not so essential after all. “We got this,” Kress said during the call. “The quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him,” Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a note to investors on Tuesday. Revenue in three months ended October 25 totaled $115.8 billion, roughly twice the amount Nvidia generated in the year ago period, and above the $109 billion expected by analysts. Net income increased 105% to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per share. The world’s leading maker of AI chips said it expects revenue in the fourth quarter to come in at $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—besting the $125 billion expected by analysts at the low point and potentially exceeding the target by billions of dollars.
